subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4! In this unit you will learn how to describe a whole set of numbers with a single, sensible value. That single value is called an average. When Amina wants to know the *typical* height of the children in her class, when a fruit seller in the Hargeisa market wants to know how many bananas a bunch *usually* holds, or when a football coach in Mogadishu wants to describe how his team *normally* scores, they are all reaching for the same idea: one number that stands for the whole group.

outcomes: Explain what an average is and why averages help us understand data.
Find the mode of a set of data – the value that appears most often – for both numbers and categories.
Recognise data sets with no mode or with more than one mode.
Find the median by arranging the data in order and locating the middle value.
Find the median when there is an even number of values by averaging the two middle numbers.
Calculate the mean by adding all the values and dividing by how many there are.
Find the range of a set of data by subtracting the smallest value from the largest.
Choose and justify which average is most useful for a particular situation.
Interpret averages in real-world problems and explain what your answer means.

concepts.title: What Is an Average?
concepts.explanation:
Imagine you and your friends are comparing how tall you are. Some are taller, some are shorter. If someone asked, “How tall are the children in your group?” you could read out every single height – but that is a long, confusing answer. Instead, you can give one number that represents the whole group. That number is an average.

An average is a way of finding the “typical” or “middle” value of a set of data. It is like a spokesperson for the whole group: one value that speaks for all of them. The clever part is that there is more than one fair way to choose that spokesperson, and each way tells you something slightly different. In this unit we study three of them – the mode, the median and the mean – and we also learn the range, which measures how spread out the data is.

concepts.title: The Mode
concepts.explanation:
Here is the great thing about the mode: you do not need to put the numbers in order first. You simply count how many times each value appears, and the one with the highest count wins. Let us walk through an example step by step.

Example: Find the mode of these test scores: 5, 3, 7, 5, 2, 5, 8.

Count how often each number appears. 5 appears 3 times; 3 appears once; 7 appears once; 2 appears once; 8 appears once.

Find the value with the highest count. The number 5 appears 3 times, which is more than any other.

The mode also works beautifully for categories – things that are not numbers at all. Suppose Khadija asks her classmates their favourite colour and records: blue, red, blue, green, blue, red, blue. Blue appears 4 times, red twice, green once, so the mode is blue. You cannot add up colours or put them in order, but you *can* count them – which is exactly why the mode is the only average that works for categories.

A real-world example: A fruit stall in Berbera has banana bunches holding these numbers of bananas: 6, 4, 5, 6, 7, 4, 4, 5, 6, 5, 7, 5. Counting carefully: 4 bananas appear 3 times, 5 bananas appear 4 times, 6 bananas appear 3 times, and 7 bananas appear twice. The mode is 5 bananas per bunch. This tells the stall owner that bunches of 5 are the most common – useful information when deciding how to price and display the fruit.
concepts.example: Two special situations are worth knowing. First, a data set can have no mode at all. In the set 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 every number appears exactly once, so no value is more common than the others – there is no mode. Second, a data set can have more than one mode. If a class vote gives Maths 8 votes and Art 8 votes, with everything else lower, then *both* Maths and Art are modes, because they tie for the most. Always count carefully so you do not miss a tie.

concepts.title: The Median
concepts.explanation:
The median is the middle value when you arrange all the numbers in order from smallest to largest. Picture your friends lining up from shortest to tallest: the person standing in the exact middle of the line represents the median height. The median does not care how big or small the numbers are – it only cares about *position*.

There is one golden rule for the median that you must never forget: always put the numbers in order first. This is the most common place learners slip up. If the numbers are jumbled, the “middle” of the jumble is meaningless – you must line them up smallest to largest before you look for the centre.

Finding the median with an odd number of values

Example: Find the median height of these students: 133 cm, 137 cm, 134 cm, 131 cm, 132 cm.

Arrange from smallest to largest: 131, 132, 133, 134, 137.

Find the middle position. There are 5 numbers, so the middle one is the 3rd value.

Cross out from both ends to check: cross 131 and 137, then 132 and 134, and 133 is left in the middle.

State the answer. The median is 133 cm.

When there is an odd number of values there is always exactly one number in the middle, and that is your median. But what happens when there is an even number of values? Then there are *two* numbers in the middle, and no single one sits at the centre. In that case, the median is the mean of the two middle numbers – you add them and divide by two.

Finding the median with an even number of values

Example: Find the median of 2, 5, 7, 9.

Check they are in order. 2, 5, 7, 9 – yes, smallest to largest.

Find the two middle numbers. With 4 values, the middle two are 5 and 7.

Add them and divide by 2. (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

State the answer. The median is 6. Notice the median need not be one of the original numbers – here 6 was not even in the list.
concepts.example: The median is especially valuable when a data set has one or two values that are very unusual – much larger or much smaller than the rest. Because the median only looks at the middle position, a single strange value cannot pull it far off. Suppose the monthly rainfall in a town is 12, 14, 13, 15, and then one flood month of 90 mm. That huge 90 barely moves the median, which still sits sensibly among the ordinary months. This is why banks often use the median to describe “typical” account balances, and why weather scientists use it for typical conditions.

concepts.title: The Mean
concepts.explanation:
The mean is the average most people think of first. To find the mean, you add up all the values and then divide by how many values there are. The mean shares the total out equally among all the data points, as if you gathered everything into one big pile and then split it fairly.

Here is a picture that makes the mean clear. Imagine five children have collected dates for iftar: 3, 5, 4, 6, and 2 dates. If they poured all their dates into one bowl and shared them out equally, how many would each child get? First find the total: 3 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 20 dates. Then share among the 5 children: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 dates each. So the mean is 4. Notice that no child actually had exactly 4 – the mean is the fair-share amount, not necessarily a real value from the list.

Example: Find the mean of these football scores: 2, 1, 3, 2, 2.

Add all the values. 2 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10.

Count how many values there are. There are 5 scores.

Divide the total by the count. 10 ÷ 5 = 2.

State the answer. The mean score is 2 goals.

Unlike the median, the mean uses every single number in the data. That is its great strength: it takes account of all the information. But it is also its weakness – because it uses every value, one very large or very small number can pull the mean a long way. If four families own 2, 3, 2, 3 goats and a fifth family owns 90 goats, the mean is (2 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 90) ÷ 5 = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 goats – yet no ordinary family owns anything close to 20. Here the mean is misleading, and the median would describe the families better. Knowing *when* the mean is trustworthy is part of becoming a good mathematician.
concepts.example: The mean does not have to be a whole number. Suppose Yusuf reads 4, 5, 5 and 6 pages on four evenings. The total is 4 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 20, and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, a tidy answer. But if he read 4, 5, 5 and 7 pages, the total is 21, and 21 ÷ 4 = 5.25 pages. A mean of “5.25 pages” is perfectly correct even though you cannot read a quarter of a page – it simply describes his typical evening's reading.

concepts.title: The Range
concepts.explanation:
The range is not an average – it does not tell you the typical or middle value. Instead, the range tells you how spread out the data is. To find the range, you subtract the smallest value from the largest value. A small range means the numbers are close together; a large range means they are far apart.

Example: A group of camels drink these amounts of water in litres: 8, 12, 9, 15, 11. The largest value is 15 and the smallest is 8, so the range is 15 − 8 = 7 litres. This tells us that from the thirstiest camel to the least thirsty, there is a gap of 7 litres.

Why is the range useful? Because two data sets can have the *same* average but be very different. Suppose two football teams both have a mean of 3 goals per match. Team A scored 3, 3, 2, 4, 3 – very steady, with a range of 4 − 2 = 2. Team B scored 0, 6, 1, 8, 0 – wildly up and down, with a range of 8 − 0 = 8. Same mean, but the range reveals that Team A is reliable while Team B is unpredictable. The range adds an important part of the story that averages alone cannot tell.
concepts.example: Take care with one thing: the range is a single number describing a *gap*, not a pair of numbers. It is wrong to say “the range is from 8 to 15.” The correct answer is “the range is 7.” Always do the subtraction to give one clear value.

concepts.title: Choosing and Interpreting the Right Average
concepts.explanation:
Now that you know the mode, median, mean and range, the real skill is deciding which to use and understanding what your answer means. Different averages can give different insights about the very same data, so a good mathematician always asks: “What is this data trying to tell me, and which tool answers my question best?”

Use the mode when you want to know what happens most often, or when you are dealing with categories such as colours, sizes or types. A shoe shop in Eastleigh choosing which size to stock most of should use the mode, because it wants the most popular size – the one that sells most frequently.

Use the median when you want the middle value and there are a few unusually high or low numbers that might mislead you. A bank describing a “typical” account balance uses the median so that a handful of very rich customers do not distort the picture.

Use the mean when you want to take account of every value and the data has no extreme outliers pulling it off course. A teacher finding the class's overall performance on a fair test often uses the mean, because it uses everybody's score.

Use the range when you want to describe how consistent or spread out the data is, usually *alongside* an average rather than instead of one. Together, an average and a range give a much fuller description than either alone.

Interpreting means explaining in plain words what the number tells you. If the mean rainfall is 14 mm, do not just write “14” – say “on a typical day this month, about 14 mm of rain fell.” Always connect your answer back to the real situation. The number is only half the work; the meaning is the other half.

You have now met four tools: the mode (most common value), the median (middle value in order), the mean (fair-share total ÷ count), and the range (largest − smallest, showing spread). These are not four separate islands – they work together to describe a set of data fully. When Halima studies the test scores of her study group, she might find the mode to see the most common mark, the median and mean to describe the typical mark from two angles, and the range to see how varied the group was.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into memory is to use them with real numbers around your home and community. Find the ages of your cousins and calculate all four measures. Record the daily high temperatures for a week and compare the mean with the median. Count how many customers visit a family stall each day and describe the results. Every time you do this, your understanding of data grows stronger, and the statistics you meet in later years will feel familiar and friendly. Now let us practise together with some fully worked examples.

methods.title: How to find the mode
steps: Count how many times each value appears (a tally helps).
Find the value with the highest count.
If two or more tie, they are all modes. If none repeats, there is no mode.

methods.title: How to find the median
methods.example: Find the median of these heights: 142, 138, 145, 140, 143.
steps: Arrange all the numbers from smallest to largest.
If there is an odd number of values, the middle one is the median.
If there is an even number, add the two middle values and divide by 2.

methods.title: How to find the mean
steps: Add up every value to get the total.
Count how many values there are.
Divide the total by the count.

methods.title: How to find the range
methods.example: Find the range of these daily temperatures in °C: 22, 25, 23, 28, 24, 26, 23.
steps: Find the largest value and the smallest value.
Subtract the smallest from the largest.
Write the answer as a single number.

methods.title: Find the range
methods.example: Find the range of these pizza sales: 45, 52, 45, 38, 67, 45, 41.
steps: The largest value is 67 and the smallest is 38.
Range = 67 − 38 = 29 pizzas.
This tells us the busiest day sold 29 more pizzas than the quietest day.

methods.title: All four measures at once
methods.example: For the scores 3, 7, 3, 9, 5, 3, 8, find the mode, median, mean and range.
steps: Mode: 3 appears 3 times, more than any other, so the mode is 3.
Median: order them — 3, 3, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9; there are 7 values, so the middle (4th) is 5.
Mean: 3 + 7 + 3 + 9 + 5 + 3 + 8 = 38, and 38 ÷ 7 = 5.43 (to two decimal places).
Range: 9 − 3 = 6.

workedExamples.title: Find the mode
workedExamples.solution: Count each value. 8 appears 4 times; 5 appears twice; 3 once; 7 once. The value with the highest count is 8. The mode is 8. Notice we did not need to sort the numbers at all — only count.

workedExamples.title: Find the median (odd number of values)
workedExamples.prompt: Find the median of these heights: 142, 138, 145, 140, 143.
workedExamples.solution: First arrange in order: 138, 140, 142, 143, 145. There are 5 values, so the middle is the 3rd. Crossing from both ends leaves 142. The median is 142 cm.

workedExamples.title: Find the median (even number of values)
workedExamples.solution: Order them: 15, 18, 22, 25. With 4 values, the two middle numbers are 18 and 22. Average them: (18 + 22) ÷ 2 = 40 ÷ 2 = 20. The median is 20.

workedExamples.title: Find the mean
workedExamples.prompt: Find the mean of these daily temperatures in °C: 22, 25, 23, 28, 24, 26, 23.
workedExamples.solution: Add them all: 22 + 25 + 23 + 28 + 24 + 26 + 23 = 171. Count the values: there are 7. Divide: 171 ÷ 7 = 24.43°C (to two decimal places). So a typical day was a little over 24°C.

workedExamples.title: Find the range
workedExamples.prompt: Find the range of these pizza sales: 45, 52, 45, 38, 67, 45, 41.
workedExamples.solution: The largest value is 67 and the smallest is 38. Range = 67 − 38 = 29 pizzas. This tells us the busiest day sold 29 more pizzas than the quietest day.

workedExamples.title: All four measures at once
workedExamples.prompt: For the scores 3, 7, 3, 9, 5, 3, 8, find the mode, median, mean and range.
workedExamples.solution: Mode: 3 appears 3 times, more than any other, so the mode is 3. Median: order them — 3, 3, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9; there are 7 values, so the middle (4th) is 5. Mean: 3 + 7 + 3 + 9 + 5 + 3 + 8 = 38, and 38 ÷ 7 = 5.43 (to two decimal places). Range: 9 − 3 = 6. So mode = 3, median = 5, mean ≈ 5.43, range = 6.

workedExamples.title: Choosing the right average
workedExamples.prompt: A shoe store sold these sizes: 6, 7, 7, 8, 7, 9, 7, 6, 7, 10. The manager can only reorder one size. Which average should guide the decision, and what is it?
workedExamples.solution: The manager wants the size that sells *most often*, so the mode is the right tool. Counting: size 7 appears 5 times, more than any other. The mode is size 7, so the manager should reorder size 7. Here the mode is far more useful than the mean or median, because the question is about popularity, not a middle value.

workedExamples.title: Working backwards from the mean
workedExamples.prompt: Omar scored a mean of 8 marks across 4 quizzes. His first three scores were 7, 9 and 8. What did he score on the fourth quiz?
workedExamples.solution: If the mean of 4 quizzes is 8, then the total must be 8 × 4 = 32 marks. His first three scores add to 7 + 9 + 8 = 24. So the fourth score is 32 − 24 = 8 marks. Working backwards from the mean like this is a powerful problem-solving skill.

activities.title: Mode Detective Around the House
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and your eyes.
steps: Choose something to count around your home – the colours of cups, the sizes of shoes by the door, or the types of fruit in the kitchen.
Make a tally as you count each type, for example: red |||, blue ||||, green |.
Find the mode – the type that appears most often.
Now find something that has no mode (every type appears the same number of times). Can you? Write down what you found.
Write one sentence: “The mode of ___ in my home is ___.” Share it with your family.

activities.title: The Median Line-Up
activities.materials: five or more family members or friends, and a tape measure or ruler (optional).
steps: Ask several people to line up from shortest to tallest.
The person standing exactly in the middle shows the median height – point to them!
If there is an even number of people, the median is halfway between the two people in the middle.
Try again using ages instead of heights. Who is the median age in your family?
This activity shows why we always put data ‘in order’ before finding the median – you are literally lining the data up.

activities.title: The Fair-Share Mean Game
activities.materials: a handful of small objects (dried beans, stones, or bottle caps) and a few small bowls or cups.
steps: Put a different number of beans into each of 4 or 5 cups – for example 3, 6, 2 and 5 beans.
Now pour all the beans together and count the total.
Share the beans out equally among the cups again. How many does each cup get?
That fair-share number IS the mean! Check it by adding your starting numbers and dividing by the number of cups.
Try it several times with different amounts. You will feel in your hands what ‘the mean’ really means: sharing the total out equally.

activities.title: Weather Data Investigation
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a way to find daily temperatures (a phone with adult help, a newspaper, or a thermometer).
steps: Record the daily high temperature for 7 days in a row.
Find the mode, median, mean and range of your week's temperatures.
Draw a simple chart with one bar for each day.
Write a short ‘weather report’: “This week the mean temperature was ___°C and the range was ___°C, so the days were mostly ___.”

activities.title: Family Survey Project
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and at least 6 family members or friends to ask.
steps: Choose a fun question, such as “How many hours did you sleep last night?” or “How many cups of tea do you drink a day?”
Collect a number from each person and write them all down.
Find the mode, median and mean of your data.
Decide which average best describes your family, and explain your choice in one or two sentences.
Present your findings as a colourful ‘family data report’ that a younger child could understand.

activities.title: Averages Puzzle Challenge
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and your thinking cap!
steps: Puzzle 1: I am thinking of 5 numbers. Their median is 12 and their mode is 8. Find at least two different sets that work.

rules.title: Key rule 1
rules.text: The Mode The mode is the value that appears MOST OFTEN. Just count each value – you do NOT need to put them in order. A set can have no mode, one mode, or several modes.

rules.title: Key rule 2
rules.text: The Median The median is the MIDDLE value once the data is in order. Always arrange smallest to largest FIRST. For an even number of values, average the two middle numbers.

rules.title: Key rule 3
rules.text: The Mean Mean = total of all values divided by how many values there are. Add them all up, then divide. The mean can be a decimal and need not match any value in the list.

rules.title: Key rule 4
rules.text: The Range Range = largest value minus smallest value. It measures SPREAD, not the average. Give one number, not a pair – do the subtraction.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in The Range.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The range is not an average – it does not tell you the typical or middle value. Instead, the range tells you how spread out the data is. To find the range, you subtract the smallest value from the largest value. A small range means the numbers are close together; a large range means they are far apart. For example, a group of camels drink these amounts of water in litres: 8, 12, 9, 15, 11. The largest value is 15 and the smallest is 8, so the range is 15 − 8 = 7 litres. This tells us that from the thirstiest camel to the least thirsty camel, the difference in water drunk was 7 litres.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Choosing and Interpreting the Right Average.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Now that you know the mode, median, mean and range, the real skill is deciding which to use and understanding what your answer means. Use the mode when you want to know what happens most often, or when you are dealing with categories such as colours, sizes or types – for example, a shoe shop deciding which size to stock most of would look at the mode. Use the median when you want the middle value and there are a few unusually high or low numbers that might mislead the mean. Use the mean when you want to share a total out equally across every value. Always check the range too, since it tells you how spread out the data is, which affects how much you can trust any single average.
